title: Percentages and applications
soi: Percentages express change and comparison relative to a whole; identifying that whole makes financial and fairness decisions more reliable.
engage: Two shops advertise different discount sequences. Which offer is genuinely cheaper, and what must a price card make clear?
atl: In order for a student to think critically, students must identify the reference quantity, test a claim with calculations and explain the limits of a financial decision.
objectives: Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages.
Interpret discounts, taxes, costs and profit in a budget.
vocabulary: per cent · reference amount · multiplier · percentage change · discount · tax · revenue · cost · gross profit · net profit

sections.title: Per cent and equivalent representations
sections.intent: Read “per cent” as “out of one hundred”, then connect fractions, decimals and percentages.
paras: A percentage is a ratio with denominator 100. 37% means 37/100 = 0.37. A percentage can exceed 100 when the amount is more than the reference whole.
To write a fraction as a percentage, find an equivalent fraction out of 100 or multiply by 100%. To write a percentage as a fraction, put it over 100 and simplify.

example.title: Connect 3/5, 0.6 and 60%
example.answer: All three name the same proportion.

sections.warning: Percentages compare to a stated whole. 50% of different totals need not be equal amounts.

practice.prompt: Write 37%, 5% and 125% as decimals.
Write 3/5, 7/20 and 1/8 as percentages.
Write 24% and 150% as fractions in simplest form.
A student says 0.5% = 0.5. Correct the statement.
In a group of 40, 18 choose football. What percentage is that?
Can a quantity be 120% of a reference amount? Give an example.
practice.answer: Yes. If the reference is 50, then 60 is 120% of it.
practice.reasoning: Percentages above 100 represent more than the reference whole.

sections.title: Finding a percentage of a quantity
sections.intent: Translate “of” into multiplication and identify the reference amount first.
paras: p% of A means p/100 × A. Useful benchmarks are 10% (divide by 10), 1% (divide by 100), 50% (halve) and 25% (quarter). Build other percentages from these.
For 15% of 240, find 10% = 24 and 5% = 12, then add: 36. Or use the multiplier 0.15 × 240 = 36.
sections.warning: A percentage is not an amount until its whole is known. 20% of 50 and 20% of 200 are different.

practice.reasoning: Use a tenth, a quarter, and a tenth plus half a tenth.

practice.prompt: Find 12.5% of 320 and 1% of 750.
Explain two ways to find 35% of 80.
practice.reasoning: Both methods use the same reference whole.

practice.prompt: A £60 jacket is reduced by 20%. Find the reduction and sale price.
Is 30% of 50 equal to 50% of 30? Explain.
practice.answer: Yes, both are 15. Multiplication can be done in either order.

practice.prompt: 15% of a number is 27. Find the number.

sections.title: Percentage increase and decrease
sections.intent: Find the change from the original amount, or use a single multiplier.
paras: An increase of p% uses multiplier 1 + p/100; a decrease uses 1 − p/100. The original amount is the reference unless the question says otherwise.
Percentage change = change/original × 100%. A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease uses 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, ending at 96% of the start.

example.title: £250 with 20% off, then 10% off
example.problem: Apply each multiplier to the current price.

sections.warning: The second percentage uses a new base. Do not add successive percentage changes unless they apply to the same unchanged whole.

practice.prompt: Increase 80 by 15% and decrease 80 by 15%.
A price rises from 50 to 60. Find the percentage increase.
Apply 20% off then 10% off to £250. Compare with 30% off.
practice.answer: £180 versus £175; the single 30% offer is £5 cheaper.

practice.prompt: Increase £100 by 20%, then decrease the result by 20%. Explain the final amount.
practice.answer: £96. The 20% decrease is £24, larger than the original £20 increase.

practice.prompt: Does reversing 10% off and 20% off change the final price?
A value falls by 20%. What percentage increase restores the original?
practice.reasoning: From 80 back to 100, the increase is 20/80 = 25%.

diagram.caption: Each multiplier acts on the current amount: 250 → 200 → 180.

sections.title: Discounts, taxes, profit and budgets
sections.intent: Separate revenue, costs and profit; apply percentages to the correct line of a budget.
paras: A discount reduces a marked price. A tax or tip usually increases a stated base. Revenue is money received; cost is money spent; profit is revenue minus all relevant costs.
For a budget, calculate each line, then add. Whole-item purchases may require rounding up. A lower unit price is not automatically a better decision if extra stock cannot be sold.

example.title: A market-stall budget
example.problem: Sell 20 honey jars at £8.10, 36 soaps at £3 and 25 jams at £5.

sections.warning: Gross profit subtracts goods cost only; net profit also subtracts fixed costs. State which profit you mean.

practice.prompt: A £9 item has 10% off. A £4 item has 25% off. Find both sale prices.
A meal costs £40 before 10% tax. Find the total.
Revenue is £395, goods cost £290 and fixed costs £63. Find gross and net profit.
A shop buys an item for £6 and sells it for £9. Is the profit 50% of cost or of selling price? Calculate both.
practice.answer: £3 profit: 50% of cost, 33 1/3% of selling price.

practice.prompt: A group needs 23 jars at £6 each. A supplier offers 30 jars at 10% off the £6 cost. Compare total outlay.
practice.reasoning: The lower unit price requires buying 7 extra jars.

practice.prompt: Fixed costs of £63 rise by 8%. With revenue £395 and goods cost £290, find the new net profit.

explore.title: Do two discounts add up?
explore.instruction: Criterion B. Use multipliers to test a rule, then explain why it holds for every starting price.
explore.intro: Offer A: 20% off, then 10% off. Offer B: 30% off. Test both on £250, £40 and £80.

items.prompt: Complete the table for £250, £40 and £80.
What single discount is equivalent to 20% then 10%? Does order matter?
items.reasoning: The product of multipliers is unchanged by order.

items.prompt: Find the combined discount for 25% then 20%.
Is there a distinct unordered pair of whole-number percentage discounts, other than 20% and 10%, giving exactly 28% off? Justify your answer.
items.answer: Yes: 4% then 25% (or 25% then 4%), since 0.96×0.75 = 0.72. The pair 10% and 20% also works but is excluded by the question.
items.reasoning: Solve (100−a)(100−b)=7200; factor pairs in range include 96×75 and 80×90.

verify.expr: [(a,b) for a in range(1,100) for b in range(a,100) if (100-a)*(100-b)==7200]

items.prompt: Write a rule for successive discounts a% and b%, and explain the base.
items.answer: Remaining multiplier (1−a/100)(1−b/100); combined discount is 1 minus this product. The second discount uses the reduced price.
items.reasoning: Multiplying multipliers tracks the changing base.

application.title: The community market stall
application.instruction: Criterion D. Simulated stall data in pounds sterling. Distinguish revenue, goods cost, fixed cost and profit.
application.intro: Expected sales: 20 honey jars, 36 soaps and 25 jams. Fixed costs are £45 for the stall and £18 for transport.

items.prompt: Find each sale price and profit per item.
items.answer: Honey £8.10, profit £2.10; soap £3.00, profit £0.50; jam £5.00, profit £1.80.
items.reasoning: Apply each discount, then subtract cost.

items.prompt: Find total revenue, goods cost, gross profit and net profit.
Next time, buy 15% more of each item, rounding up to whole items. Find the new goods cost.
Should the group accept 30 honey jars at 10% off cost instead of the 23 jars needed? Give a financial reason.
items.answer: Not on cost alone: £162 versus £138, so £24 more is tied up in stock. Accept only if extra demand or storage justifies it.
items.reasoning: Compare total outlay and risk, not just unit price.

assessment.title: The fair-price card
assessment.instruction: Criteria A and C. Design a short price card that shows the original price, discount, final price and one check.
assessment.intro: Choose one item priced at £80. Compare “25% off” with “20% off, then 5% off”.

items.prompt: Calculate both final prices and the better offer.
Write the equivalent single discount for 20% then 5%.
Give a one-sentence warning that prevents a common percentage error.
items.answer: Sample: “The second discount applies to the reduced price, so 20% and 5% do not combine to 25%.”
items.reasoning: The warning identifies the changing base.

groups.title: Mixed practice 5
groups.instruction: Connect ideas. Give units and reasons where requested.

items.prompt: Write 0.08 as a percentage.
Find 35% of 60.
Increase 120 by 5%.

A value rises from 40 to 50. Find the percentage increase.

items.answer: The final price is 25% of the original: 0.5×0.5 = 0.25.
items.reasoning: The second half is taken from the reduced price.
